title: The chipped cup
exchange: Kip holds a broken cup by its good handle. “Ise glued this. She hid the crack on the side the guests see.”
Hesper sets a saucer under it. “It held her tea for ten years. How many cups do you need a family to buy?”
Kip touches the saucer. “Could we let the next person turn it first?”
memories: Kip slips Ise’s spare key back into her pocket before he puts the cup down.
Hesper puts the apprentice’s sound little rivet beside the old glue.

editions.action: Leave the cup on its saucer at Ise’s desk
editions.reply: A visitor uses the saucer to turn the cup. Seeing the seam, he asks Ise how she'd mend his.

editions.action: Set up a repair stool at the market
editions.reply: The repair stool fills before the new cups sell. Corvan lends it his best lamp.

trusted: “Ise gave me a key. I'm going to tell her in person what we're doing with her cup.”
“If the guild will try this repair in public, they can keep their stamp on it.”

title: Who owns the rest?
exchange: Kip has written down the forest tune, including four beats of silence. “That's exactly what we heard.”
Sefa sings it with him and comes in on beat three. “My neighbour was taking a breath. Do you want to make her do it that way for ever?”
“Then give her the first turn tomorrow.” Kip tears off the top line. “I kept the other three.”
memories: Kip grins at his plain name on the supper cup and offers Sefa the clean side of the paper.
Sefa lets the rest last as long as it took her neighbour to get through the door.

editions.action: Hang Kip’s four beats under the forest blind
editions.reply: The next watcher taps four beats. When a second bird calls early, she adds its time in pencil.

editions.action: Lend the lead to the creek-blind singer
editions.reply: The creek singer speeds up the rest. A shy watcher uses the borrowed beat to join the count.

trusted: “If the Wardens want a clean copy, they can keep my crossed-out line on it.”
“Elsbet's people kept the first tune. Perhaps they'll keep this neighbour's answer too.”

title: A date for the door
exchange: “There's your date.” Kip shows Rook the morning his mother got the key. Rook holds the metal against his palm until the teeth leave marks.
“I believe that's when she got it. What if we put the following morning on the family's nameplate by mistake?”
Kip snatches the key back, then lays it on the table between them. “Write what you can use it to open.”
memories: Kip tells Rook who saved him a chair on the day the key changed hands.
Rook leaves a space on the appointment slip for the witness who was late.

editions.action: Hang the household key beside the Cold Store slip
editions.reply: The family tries the key in its drawer. Their note names the hand that passed it on and leaves the date open.

editions.action: Ask Rook to keep the dated envelope at the desk
editions.reply: A returning visitor finds two dates under the flap and can ask the family which day they remember.

trusted: “The Wardens know how to keep a key. I wish they'd learnt earlier how to give one back.”
“Elsbet's friends have offered us a second witness. We'd better save the envelope for her.”

title: What a good tool sounds like
exchange: Hesper raps a spoon and passes it to Sefa. “My old fitter gave a job to anyone who could hear that nick.”
“Even someone who couldn't hear it?” Sefa rests a thumbnail on the spoon. The buzz stops halfway along the stem.
Hesper tries the trick. “He'd have given me your job. I think I'd have taken it then.”
memories: Hesper gives the spare spoon to the apprentice who made the first blow.
Sefa hums the buzz low enough for Hesper to feel through the table.

editions.action: Take the ringing spoon to the Metalworks bench
editions.reply: A fitter with a musician's ear picks the nick out over the hum of the forge. The younger apprentices crowd in.

editions.action: Give the apprentices Sefa’s thumb test
editions.reply: A learner finds the dead patch in silence and puts a chalk ring around it for the next shift.

trusted: “They like my stamp in the guild book. I can use the space beside it to put your thumb mark in.”
“The circle keeps the sound. Could somebody also keep the chalk?”

title: The price of a shortcut
exchange: “I made a weight everyone can use today.” Hesper sets it in the butter dish. Rook weighs dish and all. “So can I. What if the customer only sees the total?”
“The cart leaves now,” she says. “I can lose a morning's pay making another one.”
Rook wipes the butter off the brass. “Would a cloth do? We'll put the empty dish on it beside the full one.”
memories: The apprentice who tried Hesper’s iron has sent a square of clean linen for the weights.
Rook keeps yesterday’s weight on the table beside the one from the second hearing.

editions.action: Send the unwrapped shop weight with the cart
editions.reply: The market takes the brass before the stall opens. Every weaver hears Hesper explain what her stamp covers.

editions.action: Send the empty dish and the weight on separate cloths
editions.reply: The cart leaves a basket behind to make room. A weaver checks the empty dish for herself before selling.

trusted: “The Seal can lend us a morning if I put the trial under my own stamp.”
“When the circle opens both accounts, leave the repairer's lost morning on the page.”

title: Who gets the last word?
exchange: Sefa has a song she only sings in the kitchen. “You wrote the words down,” she tells Rook. “Did I say you could put dinner in a library?”
Rook stands up so quickly his chair goes over. “I wanted whoever comes later to hear you.”
“You can tell them I was singing,” Sefa says at last. “You can even tell them what was for supper.”
memories: Sefa offers Rook her neighbour’s answering rest. The next verse stays folded inside her sleeve.
Rook turns the paper over and makes the family’s return address the biggest line.

editions.action: Give Sefa the only written verse
editions.reply: A visitor in the Voices hall finds a way to ask Sefa herself. The file has a date and the name of the cook.

editions.action: Leave a kitchen index without the verse
editions.reply: Two singers find each other by the index. They meet behind the listening room to decide what may be heard.

trusted: “Our correspondents let a witness correct a song. I want the right to take one home as well.”
“Two people from the circle have asked about our index. I told them they may read the envelope.”
